title: The Karaites today
hook: a small community still keeps the written Torah without the rabbinic tradition

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: secular and Jewish. Yiddishists, Bundists and secular Israelis belong through language, culture and people. What did you notice that you belong to? Today, a community whose way runs through the written text alone. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-six.

Late winter, a field of young barley. A few people walk the rows, stopping to bend down and rub the heads of grain between their fingers. Are they ripe enough? It matters, because for this community the answer helps decide when the new year of months begins, and so when Passover falls. The Torah calls that season Abib, and they go out to look for it in the field itself. These are Karaite Jews, members of a small community that has kept its own path for a very long time, and today's word is about them.
screen: `A FIELD OF YOUNG BARLEY.` → `IS IT RIPE?` → `PASSOVER WAITS ON THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: The Karaites today. The principle is simple. Karaites read the written Torah and the rest of the Hebrew Bible as the authority, without the Oral Torah that rabbinic Judaism holds alongside it, the tradition gathered in the Mishnah and the Talmud. They point to a verse in Deuteronomy: "Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it." Then a saying. Karaite tradition credits an early teacher with a line that is often paraphrased as: search the scripture well, and do not lean on my opinion. Each reader is responsible for reading. Here is what that looks like. The Torah says, "This day came ye out in the month Abib," so Karaites look to the ripening barley and the new moon for their calendar. You met this verse with the Law Committee: "Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day." Karaites have traditionally read that to mean no fire left burning on Shabbat, while rabbinic Jews read the same verse, with the Oral Torah, as allowing a light lit before Shabbat begins. Same verse, two readings. Karaite prayer also includes bowing down fully, the whole body to the ground. And the last word of today's title: today. Karaites are not a chapter in a history book. There are Karaite synagogues and families now, in Israel and elsewhere, keeping their festivals by the field and the moon. Rabbinic Jews and Karaites have argued long and hard, and a lesson like this one need not settle it. It only needs to say the plain thing: a community that reads the Torah its own way is still here.
screen: `THE WRITTEN TEXT ALONE.` · `SEARCH WELL, NOT MY OPINION.` · `BARLEY, MOON, AND NO FIRE.` · `NOT HISTORY: TODAY.` · then, large: `STILL HERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one fact about them, and let it settle. Settle, and breathe. Choose one thing from today. The barley rubbed between fingers. The Shabbat with no flame burning. The whole body bowed to the ground in prayer. Hold that one picture. Notice what it would be like to keep it, week after week, as a small community, faithfully, while the neighbors around you do something else. Stay with that one picture, without adding anything to it. The bell holds the time.
The Karaites today. A small Jewish community that keeps the written Torah as its authority, without the rabbinic Oral Torah, and is still keeping it now. Today's word.
Your line: still here. Today, read one short passage of something that matters to you for yourself, slowly, before you check what anyone else says about it. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Karaite Jews keep the commandments of the Hebrew Bible as they read them directly, set their calendar by the new moon and the ripening barley, and pray in their own synagogues, including full prostration.

notes: The 'search well in the Torah and do not rely on my opinion' saying is attributed by tradition to Anan ben David; the lesson does not name him and says 'Karaite tradition credits an early teacher'. Confirm.

Karaite calendar (Abib/barley and the new moon), the traditional reading of Exodus 35:3 (no fire left burning), and full prostration in prayer: confirm these describe current Karaite practice fairly; practice may vary today.
'In Israel and elsewhere' avoids any count or location claim; confirm.
The note that the name קָרָאִים is 'usually linked to reading scripture' (mikra) is an etymology; confirm with a standard source.
